introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 2 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Answer FIVE questions, choosing AT LEAST TWO from each section. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FIVE questions, choosing AT LEAST TWO from each section » (5 en tout, au moins 2 par section). `regles_choix` ne sait exprimer que « n parmi m » : chaque section porte la règle minimale (2 sur 4) ; la règle « 5 en tout » n'est pas exprimable et figure dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : le sujet imprime les points de chaque partie (a) et (b), jamais le total de la question ; `points` de l'exercice est donc laissé vide. Les parties totalisent 20 pour chaque question (10+10, 10+10, 10+10, 10+10, 12+8, 12+8, 12+8, 8+12), conformément à « All questions carry equal marks ». Aucun écart constaté.

Sujet scanné (filigrane gcerevision.com en travers de la page ; sur la page de garde, le texte du verso apparaît en transparence, en miroir) : l'ensemble reste lisible. Titre, niveau (ADVANCED LEVEL), code 0725, session JUNE 2026 et durée (trois heures) vérifiés sur la page de garde. Le sujet ne compte que deux pages : page de garde, puis les huit questions (Section A : 1 à 4 ; Section B : 5 à 8) sur une seule page.

Défaut d'impression : à la question 5(b) la lettre « (b) » est maculée (« (ḅ) ») ; lue comme (b) d'après la séquence (a), (b). Le numéro « 2 » en en-tête de page de garde est imprimé de façon approximative (« Economics 2 »).

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont rédigés (niveau Advanced). Les exemples chiffrés (TVA au taux hypothétique de 20 %, chaîne cacao 100 000 / 160 000 / 250 000 / 320 000 FCFA, élasticité de -0,5) sont hypothétiques et recalculés avec Python ; le taux de 20 % n'est pas le taux légal camerounais. Aucune statistique réelle n'est avancée.

Figures : trois schémas produits avec matplotlib (Q2 fig-1 prix agricoles à demande inélastique, Q2 fig-2 stock régulateur, Q6 fig-1 encaisses d'activité et de spéculation). Ils illustrent les corrigés ; le sujet n'imprime aucune figure. Les courbes sont schématiques, sans échelle chiffrée.
Question 6(a) : « diagram(s) » demandé par le sujet ; le diagramme est décrit dans le corrigé et fourni en figure (Keynes : L1 fonction du revenu, L2 fonction du taux d'intérêt, trappe à liquidité).

questions.enonce_markdown: Why are trade unions desired in modern industries? (10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A **trade union** is an organisation of workers formed to protect and promote their interests, particularly through **collective bargaining** with employers. In modern industries, where firms are large, employ many workers and use advanced technology, an individual worker has very little bargaining power. Trade unions are therefore desired for the following reasons.

1. **Collective bargaining over wages.** A union negotiates for all its members together. The workers' combined strength is far greater than that of one worker, who can easily be replaced. This helps to raise wages and to keep them in line with productivity and the cost of living.
2. **Better working conditions.** Unions press for reasonable working hours, safety and health standards, protective clothing, holidays, sick leave, maternity leave and breaks.
3. **Job security.** Unions defend workers against unfair or arbitrary dismissal and negotiate redundancy pay and retraining when machines replace workers.
4. **Countering the power of employers (monopsony).** Large modern firms may be the sole or dominant employer in an area. A union balances this power, so that wages are not forced below the value of the workers' productivity.
5. **Representation and settlement of disputes.** Unions represent workers in grievances and disciplinary cases and provide a channel of communication with management. Peaceful negotiation reduces the number of strikes and misunderstandings.
6. **Welfare and social benefits.** Unions provide legal aid, strike pay, loans, insurance, funeral grants, pensions and sickness benefits for members and their families.
7. **Training and education of workers.** Many unions offer training and information, which raise skill and productivity, and help workers to adapt to new technology.
8. **Participation in management and decision making.** Unions allow workers to take part in decisions affecting them, such as the introduction of new machines, which may raise productivity and loyalty.
9. **Political and social influence.** Through lobbying, unions influence labour laws, minimum wage legislation, social security and tax policy, and they speak for workers on national issues, often taking part in discussions with the government and employers' associations.
10. **Fair treatment and equality.** Unions work against discrimination, child labour and abuses by employers, and promote equal opportunities.

**Evaluation.** Trade unions are not without disadvantages: excessive wage demands can raise costs and prices, cause unemployment or discourage investment; strikes cause losses in output; and unions may protect inefficient workers or use their power to benefit members at the expense of the unemployed (insiders and outsiders). Nevertheless, when responsible, they remain desired to protect workers and promote industrial peace.

**Conclusion.** Trade unions are desired in modern industries because they give workers collective strength in bargaining, protect jobs and working conditions, provide welfare services and represent workers' views in management and in national policy.

questions.enonce_markdown: Under what circumstances might a trade union secure increased earnings for its members? (10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A trade union may raise the earnings (wages and fringe benefits) of its members above the level that would exist without bargaining, but its success depends on the conditions in which it operates. Wage increases are easier to obtain where the **loss of jobs caused by a higher wage is small** and where the employer is **willing or able to pay**. The following circumstances favour the union.

1. **Inelastic demand for labour.** If demand for labour is price-inelastic, a rise in the wage leads to a proportionately smaller fall in employment, so total earnings of the group rise. Demand for labour is inelastic when: (i) **labour cost is a small proportion of total cost** (so that a wage rise adds little to the price of the product); (ii) **substitutes for labour (machines or other workers) are not easily available** or are costly; (iii) **demand for the final product is inelastic**, so that the employer can pass the higher cost on to consumers without losing many sales. (These are the **Marshall-Hicks rules** of derived demand.)
2. **High level of union membership and solidarity.** A union that organises most workers in the industry (as in a closed shop) and whose members are loyal and willing to strike has strong bargaining power, since the employer cannot easily replace the strikers.
3. **Scarcity of the skills of members.** Workers with rare or highly specialised skills (pilots, surgeons, electricians in a power company) are hard to replace, so the union has strong bargaining power.
4. **Rising productivity and profitability of the firm.** When output per worker, sales and profits are rising, the union can argue that wage claims are affordable and justified, and the firm is more willing to pay. A firm earning high (supernormal) profits can pay more without cutting employment.
5. **Growing demand for the product or for labour.** In a boom, when unemployment is low and firms compete for scarce workers, the union's bargaining position is stronger.
6. **High cost of strikes to the employer.** Where production is perishable, time-sensitive or depends on continuous processes (oil refining, ports, electricity, transport), a strike is very costly, and employers prefer to settle quickly.
7. **Monopsony (single buyer of labour).** Where a union faces a monopsonist employer, a wage set above the monopsony wage may raise both the wage **and** employment, up to the point where the union wage equals the marginal revenue product of labour (bilateral monopoly).
8. **Strong strike funds and public support.** Financial reserves allow members to hold out in a long dispute, and public sympathy puts pressure on the employer or government to settle.
9. **Favourable government policy and legislation.** Laws that protect the right to organise and to strike, recognition of unions, minimum wage laws and government willingness to act as a mediator or to be a sympathetic employer (in the public sector) help the union.
10. **Competent leadership and negotiation skills.** Well-informed union officials, with good research and bargaining techniques, can make a more convincing case.
11. **Inflation and rising cost of living.** Workers can claim wage rises to keep up with rising prices, and employers often accept them where all firms are affected.
12. **Where the industry is protected from competition** (for example, a monopoly or a protected industry), the employer can pass on higher wage costs to consumers.

**Evaluation.** A successful wage claim can have costs: it may cause unemployment of some workers (outsiders), raise prices, reduce the competitiveness of the firm and encourage the replacement of workers by machines in the longer run. Where unemployment is high and the labour supply is abundant, as in many developing countries, and where the informal sector is large, the union's power is weaker.

**Conclusion.** A trade union is most likely to win higher earnings where the demand for its members' labour is inelastic, membership is strong, the firm is profitable, the economy is expanding, and the law and public opinion are on its side.
